item.title: Asian-American Deli Café Hestia Signs 8K-SF Lease at 570 Lexington Avenue
item.dc:creator: Mark Hallum
item.description: A cafe serving Asian and American cuisine is opening a fourth Manhattan location, Commercial Observer has learned. Café Hestia, a group of family-run delis, has signed a 20-year, 8,000-square-foot lease at the base of the Feil Organization’s 570 Lexington Avenue, which it will likely also use as a catering facility, according to tenant broker Kassin […]
item.content:encoded:
A cafe serving Asian and American cuisine is opening a fourth Manhattan location, Commercial Observer has learned.

Café Hestia, a group of family-run delis, has signed a 20-year, 8,000-square-foot lease at the base of the Feil Organization’s 570 Lexington Avenue, which it will likely also use as a catering facility, according to tenant broker Kassin Sabbagh Realty (KSR).

KSR did not immediately disclose the asking rent, but the average asking rent for the nearby retail corridor along Fifth Avenue from East 42nd to East 49th streets was $575 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE.

“Our strategy has remained focused on finding operators that create lasting value for our tenants and the surrounding neighborhood, and Café Hestia builds on that vision with its all-day dining concept and wide variety of offerings,” Jordan Goldblum, director of retail leasing at the Feil Organization, said in a statement.

Goldblum and Randall Briskin negotiated on behalf of the landlord in-house, while KSR’s Albert Manopla and Jack Khaski handled the deal for Café Hestia.

KSR did not immediately provide a comment.

Café Hestia’s other Manhattan locations are at 686 Third Avenue by Grand Central Terminal, 513 Seventh Avenue near Pennsylvania Station, and 80 Maiden Lane in the Financial District.

Other tenants in the 50-story landmarked skyscraper on Lexington Avenue, also known as the General Electric Building, include international litigation firm Wolf Popper, which signed a 13,400-square-foot lease in December 2025, as well as the Real Estate Board of New York, which has a 23,031-square-foot office.

Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Edgewood Capital Provides $28M Refi for Fort Lauderdale Condo Project
item.dc:creator: Andrew Coen
item.description: Latitude Group has landed a $27.9 million loan to refinance a newly completed condominium project in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Edgewood Capital supplied the loan for the Terraces condo tower set to debut this fall, sources familiar with the deal told CO. Latitude Group previously secured a $24.5 million construction loan from […]
item.content:encoded:
Latitude Group has landed a $27.9 million loan to refinance a newly completed condominium project in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned.

Edgewood Capital supplied the loan for the Terraces condo tower set to debut this fall, sources familiar with the deal told CO. Latitude Group previously secured a $24.5 million construction loan from Linkvest Capital in June 2024 to build the 22-unit development at 527 Orton Avenue, The Real Deal reported at the time. 

BayBridge Real Estate Capital arranged the refi with a team consisting of AJ Felberbaum, Jay Miller, Spencer Miller and Noah Rothman. 

Latitude acquired the half-ace development site for the project in 2020 for $3.3 million, according to TRD, citing property records. 

Sixty percent of the condos at the Terraces have been sold, according to the property’s website. The property’s amenities include a fitness center, a yoga studio, a swimming pool, cabanas and a community kitchen. 

Edgewood Capital, Latitude Group and BayBridge Real Estate Capital did not immediately return requests for comment.

Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Decron Properties Buys 163-Unit Property in L.A.’s Miracle Mile for $114M
item.dc:creator: Gregory Cornfield
item.description: Decron Properties has acquired a 163-unit property in Los Angeles’ Miracle Mile for $114 million as the firm’s first L.A. deal in nearly two years. The Los Angeles-based investment firm acquired the asset at 5550 Wilshire Boulevard, a residential and retail property developed in 2010, at what Decron described as a substantial discount to replacement […]
item.content:encoded:
Decron Properties has acquired a 163-unit property in Los Angeles’ Miracle Mile for $114 million as the firm’s first L.A. deal in nearly two years.

The Los Angeles-based investment firm acquired the asset at 5550 Wilshire Boulevard, a residential and retail property developed in 2010, at what Decron described as a substantial discount to replacement cost. After focusing on Sun Belt markets, the firm said it continues to pursue opportunities across Los Angeles, San Jose, Orange County, San Diego and Seattle as well. 

“Our growth-market strategy has never been a referendum on Los Angeles,” Decron President and CEO David Nagel said in a statement. “For a period, the risk-adjusted returns here simply weren’t competitive with what we were finding in the Sun Belt markets.”

Nagel added that Los Angeles remains “one of the nation’s most important and chronically undersupplied housing markets,” where new supply is difficult and expensive to build. 

5550 Wilshire includes one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments and townhomes. Amenities include a pool and spa, a resident lounge, a private movie theater and rooftop lounges. The property also includes 14,686 square feet of ground-floor retail that is fully leased to tenants that include Chipotle, Five Guys and FedEx Office. 

JLL’s Blake Rogers represented both Decron and the seller in the transaction.

Decron owns and manages nearly 10,000 multifamily units and about 1 million square feet of retail across California, Washington and Arizona, with a portfolio totaling roughly 8.7 million square feet.

Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Corebridge Financial Refis Meatpacking Office Property With $293M Loan
item.dc:creator: Andrew Coen
item.description: A joint venture between Aurora Capital Associates and William Gottlieb Real Estate has sealed a $293 million loan to refinance a mixed-use asset in Manhattan’s Meatpacking District, according to a release. Corebridge Financial provided the fixed-rate, permanent loan on the 158,957-square-foot building at 40 10th Avenue. The 2019-built property features 112,241 square feet of office […]
item.content:encoded:
A joint venture between Aurora Capital Associates and William Gottlieb Real Estate has sealed a $293 million loan to refinance a mixed-use asset in Manhattan’s Meatpacking District, according to a release.

Corebridge Financial provided the fixed-rate, permanent loan on the 158,957-square-foot building at 40 10th Avenue. The 2019-built property features 112,241 square feet of office space and 46,176 square feet of retail on the first two floors.

Walker & Dunlop negotiated the debt with a team consisting of Dustin Stolly, Aaron Appel, Jonathan Schwartz, Keith Kurland, Adam Schwartz, Sean Reimer, Jordan Casella and Stanley Cayre. 

“40 10th Avenue stands out in building quality, location and experience — all elements that differentiate a property for tenants,” Stolly, senior managing director of the capital markets institutional advisory team at Walker & Dunlop, said in a statement. “The fully leased office component, institutional tenant roster and substantial outdoor space demonstrate the continued demand for high-touch, well-located workplaces in New York.”

The 10-story building has office tenants that include Starwood Capital Group, WestCap Management, RTW Investments, Stripes and Checkout.com. The retail portion of the property is occupied by Hyundai Motor. 

The property is positioned for success, according to Walker & Dunlop, since the 

Meatpacking District is one of Manhattan’s most supply-constrained office and retail submarkets.

Aurora Capital Associates and William Gottlieb Real Estate landed a $150 million loan from 

Deutsche Pfandbriefbank in June 2020  to refinance construction debt to build the property, CO first reported at the time. 

Corebridge Financial, Aurora Capital and William Gottlieb Real Estate did not immediately return requests for comment.

Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Stroller Brand Uppababy Relocates Store to 156 Montague Street in Brooklyn Heights
item.dc:creator: Mark Hallum
item.description: Known for its distinctive strollers, baby gear brand Uppababy is relocating its store within Brooklyn, Commercial Observer has learned. The high-end baby accessories brand is opening a 3,780-square-foot brick-and-mortar location at Owen Realty’s 156 Montague Street in Brooklyn Heights, according to broker JLL. Uppababy will move next year from 90 Smith Street in Cobble Hill, […]
item.content:encoded:
Known for its distinctive strollers, baby gear brand Uppababy is relocating its store within Brooklyn, Commercial Observer has learned.

The high-end baby accessories brand is opening a 3,780-square-foot brick-and-mortar location at Owen Realty’s 156 Montague Street in Brooklyn Heights, according to broker JLL. Uppababy will move next year from 90 Smith Street in Cobble Hill, where it established its Brooklyn retail and service “hub” in about 2019.

JLL did not immediately provide the length of the lease or the asking rent for the space, but the average retail asking rent along nearby Fulton Street was $190 per square foot in 2025, according to the most recent retail report from the Real Estate Board of New York. 

“Brooklyn is an important market for Uppababy, and this relocation allows us to build on the relationships we have developed with local families,” Bob Monahan, co-founder and CEO of Uppababy, said in a statement. “Brooklyn Heights has a strong community of young and growing families, and the Montague Street location gives us the space and accessibility to deliver the hands-on product experience and personalized service that define our hub stores.”

Uppababy manufactures and sells strollers, car seats, highchairs and other products for infants. Its top-of-the-line Vista V3 stroller, described on the company’s website as a “best seller,” retails for $1,000.

JLL’s Jesse Wolff and Elijah Mehl represented the tenant in the transaction while Ryan Condren and George Danut, also from JLL, negotiated on behalf of Owen Realty.

Owen Realty, which uses the LLC Montague Realty Development Associates, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Montague Street offers the neighborhood density, visibility and accessibility that work well for family focused retailers like Uppababy,” Wolff said in a statement.

Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Institutional and Private Equity Investors: Their Commercial Real Estate Hot Takes
item.dc:creator: Brian Pascus
item.description: Commercial Observer’s annual Institutional Investor & Private Equity Forum took center stage at 237 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan on Sept. 16, when some of the biggest names in commercial real estate investment offered their thoughts on the state of capital markets. Under the shadow of the Federal Reserve set to raise short-term interest rates […]
item.content:encoded:
Commercial Observer’s annual Institutional Investor & Private Equity Forum took center stage at 237 Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan on Sept. 16, when some of the biggest names in commercial real estate investment offered their thoughts on the state of capital markets. 

Under the shadow of the Federal Reserve set to raise short-term interest rates for the first time in three years (which they did that very afternoon), Blackstone’s Katie Keenan, global head of core-plus real estate and CEO of Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT), sat down with Jennifer Recine, partner at King & Spalding, to host the opening keynote. 

Keenan enumerated reasons why the U.S. market is currently experiencing “a compelling backdrop for real estate” largely from an ongoing reset in asset values, a growth in cash flows, and the supply in asset classes such as multifamily and retail at the lowest levels in decades. She also touched on the accelerating demand from artificial intelligence, digitalization, and e-commerce.

“When you have growing demand and flat, or down, supply, it’s a meaningful impact on what you see from a cash flow and growth perspective,” Keenan said. “The debt capital markets … are as healthy as I’ve seen them in a long time. Capital is readily available and it’s well priced.” 

Keenan noted that 90 percent of Blackstone’s core-plus portfolio consists of logistics, data centers and multifamily, and that these assets benefit from the conservative approach that core-plus investing uniquely prioritizes. 

“It’s driven by that cash-flow growth, it doesn’t rely on leverage, it’s a lower leverage strategy,” she said. “And it’s not about cap-rate compression. … This is really about buying good assets that can compound over time and deliver a significant portion of their return along the way.”

Keenan closed her remarks by touting BREIT’s 10-year track record of market performance, noting that the private real estate investment trust has delivered 9.4 percent net return over the last 10 years, which is 35 percent higher than the public REIT market. 

“It really does what real estate is supposed to do in a broader portfolio: It provides diversification, non-correlation, cash flow, stability, and compounded returns,” she said. “The proof is in the performance.”

The morning’s second panel, moderated by King & Spalding’s James Stull, examined the state of institutional real estate and where capital is moving today. 

Greg MacKinnon, head of research at Pension Real Estate Association, began by offering a humorous assessment of the market, which he compared to a patient “out of intensive care, but still in the hospital undergoing observation.” 

He emphasized that CRE is well past the worst of the higher interest rates and regional banking crises that plagued 2022 and 2023, and that bright spots can be found in senior housing and retail, due to supply shortages. 

“But all other sectors are clumped together with expected unlevered returns of low sixes [6 percent], which is fine, but it’s not exactly exciting,” he said. “You’re not going to write a letter home to your mother about 6 percent returns in real estate.”

Adriana de Alcantara, senior managing director and fund manager at Hines U.S. Property Partners, boasted of an aggressive approach her firm has taken in the last two years, noting that Hines has invested $1 billion into its open-ended institutional fund and another $1 billion into its non-traded REIT. 

“It’s all about income and basis, buying the right assets at the right basis,” she said. “Real estate is less complicated than people think: As long as you buy in the right location and at the right price, you’re going to be fine.” 

Miles Treaster, president of Americas capital markets at Cushman & Wakefield, outlined what he described as “a paradigm shift” in the current market, as CRE investment participants are gradually starting to accept that the go-go times of the 2010s — when asset values constantly went up and the cost of capital and raising funds always went down — is not returning anytime soon. 

But he pointed to alternatives like data centers and senior housing as examples of strong performance.

“There’s been a lot of resiliency in this market, which, if you told me oil would be above $100 per barrel and rates would be above 5 percent on the 10-Year, I’d say you’re crazy,” he joked. “But the S&P 500 and the companies in it are doing quite well, and real estate usually follows.” 

Starwood Property Trust President Jeff DiModica took a decidingly more cautious  tone, stating outright that the move of long-term interest rates into 5 percent territory is something the market will need to digest while dealing with hundreds of billions of dollars worth of debt tied to data center development, which he called “a big driver to this 5 percent — there’s just not enough buyers of duration in the market.”

DiModica said that in previous eras the market could still perform well under high interest rates because of strong growth, property cash flows, and rising incomes. But he’s afraid the party is now over in that respect. 

“I’m a little afraid we might not have that here,” he said. “Rate moves are typically bad for real estate, as real estate is typically very levered to interest rates, and I think that will show its teeth. We haven’t worked through a lot of the problems of the post-COVID, 2022 [era].” 

The third panel of the morning, moderated by Dan Berman, partner at HSF Kramer, focused on the difference between domestic and foreign investment trends and where emerging opportunities can be found. 

Shawn Lese, chief investment officer and head of funds management at Nuveen Real Estate, said that it has only been in the last 18 months that it’s been possible to raise institutional capital in generous amounts, and that his firm has been able to secure investment from different corners of the globe. 

“We’ve been raising money from Canada, from Germany, from Australia,” said Lese. “What we’ve consistently heard from those large state plans, sovereign wealth funds, superannuation funds, is basically, ‘We’re underallocated, we’re underallocated [into commercial real estate].’” 

Gordon Black, executive vice president and portfolio manager of private equity at Heitman, argued that the investment climate has “gone from paralysis to selectivity,” and that traditional CRE now needs to compete with more products in the real assets space, namely infrastructure development and assets tangentially related to data centers. 

“It’s a relative world and real estate has to perform, it’s got to be somewhere between fixed-income and equities, and right now that’s a problem,” Black said. “There’s been a lack of new capital in lower-risk strategies, and I think a lot of that’s tied to [a lack of] transaction volume.” 

Dwight Angelini, co-founder and managing partner at Longpoint Partners, said commercial real estate might be awash in capital today, but it is still weighed down by the reputational harm it suffered from the exuberance and poor underwriting that occurred after 2019 and before 2023.

“You had all this capital come in, it was easy, everyone is raising [capital] and getting into different sectors, and real estate was the new venture capital or private equity,” said Angelini. “So a lot of dumb things were done between 2019 and 2023, and real estate, on some level, has reputation problems that need to be fixed.” 

Richard Prokup, U.S. CEO of Mapletree, cataloged where he’s seen aggressive foreign investing, singling out Australia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and Singapore as countries that have been willing to pour capital into domestic CRE. Conversely, he noted that in recent years Middle Eastern nations have pulled out of U.S. investment, but the war in Iran has now caused them to seek safe haven in the States. 

“The war in the Middle East has actually helped us because money that those organizations had earlier earmarked locally now can’t be deployed,” Prokup said. “So that money has to shift somewhere, and, if it has to shift, a portion of it, very likely, has come to the U.S.”

Lese added that “the U.S. is the only solid, investable place on the planet right now.” 

After a short break, discussion resumed with Commercial Observer Executive Editor Cathy Cunningham and Citrin Cooperman’s Mark Mindick holding a keynote discussion with Bert Crouch, partner and head of real estate equity at Apollo Global Management. 

Crouch began by outlining the reasons behind his firm’s August 2025 take-private acquisition of Bridge Investment Group, a move that transferred $50 billion in assets from Bridge’s alternatives business to Apollo. It ended up as the largest inorganic expansion that Apollo has ever made, doubling its real estate equity assets to over $110 billion.  

“That was really the catalyst for me to appreciate that Apollo was now all-in on real estate,” said Crouch. “There’s a complementary nature of the platform. … [Bridge] is middle market, so if our bold bracket [debt] business under Scott Weiner and Apollo is doing $130 million average loan size, Bridge is doing $30 million, so their middle-market business complements it really well.”

Crouch emphasized that Apollo’s “secular thematic convictions” are in senior living and housing, namely the demographic shifts into senior housing, health care real estate, and industrialization in e-commerce and logistics as well as defense contracting and semiconductor chip production. 

“When we settled on those themes, they’re not just real estate themes, they’re Apollo themes, across real estate equity and private credit,” said Crouch. 

  

The fourth discussion centered around private credit and new fund formation and was moderated by Frank Ditta, director at law firm Goulston & Storrs. 

Brian Flax, executive vice president at Meridian Capital Group, noted that special situation deals that needed to be financed before the interest rates increase will still seek rescue financing in the months ahead, and that opportunistic buyers looking to pounce on distress will also be in the market for acquisition credit. 

“There is going to be no shortage of private credit available, because the capital has been raised and needs to be put to work,” Flax said. “It will all be a matter of where it will go.” 

Russell Young, executive vice president of investment management at RXR, outlined how his firm is both an owner-developer as well as a capital solutions provider, and emphasized in his own remarks that the credit landscape is changing very quickly, creating room for hybrid players. 

“The definition between equity and debt is blurring at this point,” said Young. “We’re really charting new territory in that regard.”

Nicholas Baccile, director at Canyon Partners Real Estate, pointed out that creativity is paramount in forming capital stacks, especially in an era when private credit competes with traditional lenders. 

“It’s not just cut and dried like your debt is 65 percent and you have common equity. It’s maybe you’re going up to 80 percent loan-to-cost and you are competing with other debt funds and therefore your cost of capital is a certain way,” explained Baccile. “That creativity is what will differentiate a lot of groups going forward.”

Matt Jones, chief investment officer at Harbor Group International, used his time to emphasize that now is the moment for private capital to win business over traditional lending groups. 

“Maybe rates go up and agencies and insurance companies stick to a sizing program and can only offer a B note,” explained Jones. “So this is where private capital should get paid a premium to provide a solution — I think the opportunity set over the next 12 months is tremendous.” 

The morning’s final discussion, hosted by Andrew Dansker, CEO of mortgage brokerage Dansker Group, examined shifting allocations and how institutional investors are rebalancing their real estate portfolios. 

Trisha Connolly Horowitz, head of CRE finance at Catal Capital, admitted that her firm has gone from seeing 10 to 15 deals per day to four or five amid the interest rate hikes, but said she believes there’s money to be made within the middle market. 

“For me, as a lender, there’s always a good borrower for a $10 million to $15 million size deal,” she said. “We continue to see transaction volume in the middle-market space.”

Morris Betesh, founder and managing partner at Arrow Real Estate Advisors, said most of the business he has seen these days has been on maturing loans and motivated sellers.

“Specific to us, 70 percent of our business in the last 12 months was floating-rate [debt],” he said. “We represent a lot of developers doing value-add financings, where the outlook is two to three years from now, and there’s still optimism in the market that the experience we’re having today … is short term.” 

Stephany Chen, senior vice president of investor relations at Trinity Investments, used the hospitality space as an example of rebalancing, emphasizing the operationally intense nature of those assets and how much they require experienced operators to reach outperformance. 

“We’re definitely seeing more interest in the hospitality space,” she said. “The trend is those who are understanding the fundamentals, the operational focus of the asset, are being able to invest in the sector.”

The forum closed with observations by William Pattison, head of real estate research and strategy at MetLife Investment Management, on which sectors he believes will become institutionalized in the coming years.  

“I think 10 years from now senior housing and medical office will be as institutionalized as apartments and industrial areas are today,” he said. “Diversified funds that are not in those segments probably won’t survive.” 

Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: A Different Downtown San Diego Is Taking Shape
item.dc:creator: Gregory Cornfield
item.description: Downtown San Diego looks a lot different than it did a year ago. People who haven’t spent much time there recently may still picture the challenges that dominated conversations before: quiet streets, empty storefronts, concerns about safety, and office towers that have too much vacant space. Some of those challenges remain. Office vacancy is still […]
item.content:encoded:
Downtown San Diego looks a lot different than it did a year ago.

People who haven’t spent much time there recently may still picture the challenges that dominated conversations before: quiet streets, empty storefronts, concerns about safety, and office towers that have too much vacant space.

Some of those challenges remain. Office vacancy is still a real issue with recent estimates in the 20 percent range as employers rethink their space needs amid hybrid work models.

But some things have changed. Downtown increasingly feels like it has reached a turning point. The question isn’t whether it will recover, but how it will recover, and what progress is already underway.

One reason for the improvement is that momentum isn’t coming from a single source. Businesses, residents, visitors, universities, cultural institutions, philanthropy and new investment are all contributing to the area’s revival.

The Downtown San Diego Partnership, for example, has made cleaner, safer and more welcoming streets a priority. The Clean & Safe team serves six Downtown neighborhoods over 1.15 square miles, 280 blocks and more than 13,000 unique parcels within the Property and Business Improvement District.

Organizations like the Prebys Foundation are also making significant investments in downtown real estate and public life. Prebys recently acquired the long-vacant California Theater site for $6.3 million, purchased major office properties including Wells Fargo Plaza and a Little Italy headquarters, and partnered on a grand Civic Center redesign.

Its investment in the historic 24-story 401 B Street tower, for example, is particularly telling. The foundation described the acquisition as “a declaration of belief in what downtown can become: a vibrant hub of commerce, culture and civic life that welcomes all who call this region home and all who are drawn to its promise.”

Educational and cultural institutions are adding another layer of activity. The San Diego Symphony, for example, draws people into the urban core for performances at the Rady Shell at Jacobs Park and Copley Symphony Hall. UC San Diego operates Park & Market, a four-story hub for education, arts and community programming, while initiatives such as ArtsConnect are expanding the university’s cultural presence downtown.

Visitors are returning in significant numbers, too. According to the San Diego Tourism Authority, the San Diego Convention Center hosted 61 conventions with 550,000 attendees in 2025. That translates to 1.29 million of contracted hotel room nights as well as $884.5 million in attendee spending that year alone.

None of these investments can transform Downtown San Diego on their own, but together they change how a city feels. And that matters.

People experience cities at street level. They notice whether sidewalks are comfortable, parks are maintained, storefronts are open, if there are places to sit, and if other people are around. Those details shape whether someone enjoys spending time downtown and, just as importantly, whether they have a reason to return.

That is why investments in public space matter so much. East Village Green, an approximately 2.1-acre community park planned for the East Village neighborhood, is one example of how new public space can strengthen the surrounding area.

Horton Plaza Park offers another. The 1.8-acre public square at Fourth Avenue and Broadway is expected to reopen, restoring a prominent gathering place near the Gaslamp Quarter. Spaces like these give people reasons to spend time downtown that have nothing to do with reporting to an office.

Creating places where residents, workers, students and visitors can overlap is how healthy downtowns are built.

Even the struggling office market may create opportunities. Many downtown buildings have changed hands in recent years at prices well below their previous valuations. A lower cost basis can give new owners flexibility that previous investors lacked to offer more competitive rents, modernize buildings, improve amenities and rethink how older properties fit into a changing downtown.

Downtown also has something many other employment centers cannot easily replicate. Thousands of people already live within walking distance of offices, restaurants, transit, entertainment and cultural amenities, while trolley and bus connections link the urban core with the broader region.

That points to an even bigger opportunity. San Diego does not need to re-create the downtown of 2019, built primarily around the rhythms of the office workweek. It can build something stronger.

Resilient downtowns don’t depend on a single industry, population or schedule. They give people different reasons to be there at different times: to work, live, learn, eat, attend a concert, visit a park, go to a convention or simply spend an afternoon.

Downtown San Diego is not finished. It still needs more employers, retail and investment, along with sustained attention to cleanliness and safety. Office vacancy won’t disappear overnight, and neither will perceptions formed during more difficult years.

But a year ago, many of the pieces needed for recovery weren’t moving in the same direction. Today, they are. That doesn’t mean Downtown San Diego is going back to what it was, but it does create an opportunity to build toward something better.

David McCullough is principal landscape architect and founder of McCullough Landscape Architecture.

item.title: BridgeInvest Provides $114M Refi for Robert Rivani ‘Concierge Office’ in Miami Beach
item.dc:creator: Brian Pascus
item.description: Developer Robert Rivani has secured $114.3 million to refinance his eponymous Rivani, a 165,170-square-foot office and retail complex on Miami Beach, Commercial Observer can first report. BridgeInvest provided the debt out of its BridgeInvest Credit Fund V, where the new capital will retire $38 million of existing debt used to renovate the property and finance […]
item.content:encoded:
Developer Robert Rivani has secured $114.3 million to refinance his eponymous Rivani, a 165,170-square-foot office and retail complex on Miami Beach, Commercial Observer can first report. 

BridgeInvest provided the debt out of its BridgeInvest Credit Fund V, where the new capital will retire $38 million of existing debt used to renovate the property and finance leasing costs through stabilization. Berkadia’s Brad Williamson, Scott Wadler, Mitch Sinberg and Matthew Robbins arranged the transaction. 

“Robert took a well-located but conventional office asset and created something that simply didn’t exist in this market,” said Williamson. “The leasing velocity and caliber of tenants demonstrate the demand for a differentiated workplace experience.”

Located at 1691 Michigan Avenue, the seven-story Rivani building includes 119,000 square feet of office space and more than 43,000 square feet of retail space.

The asset is currently 83 percent leased and already serves as the 20,000 square-foot global headquarters for Playboy Enterprises. It features an office and retail tenant base that includes Apple, Morgan Stanley, Wix, The Jills Zeder Group, World Red Eye and Monarch Athletic Club. 

Robert Rivani acquired the property in 2024 for $62.5 million, before integrating hospitality amenities such as a full-service concierge and valet, a spa and fitness area, a meditation room, a podcast studio and a speakeasy-style lounge into what has been a traditional office asset. 

Rivani’s next step for the asset requires voter approval. He hopes Miami Beach voters will approve a $50 million expansion of the property above an existing parking garage that would allow him to build an additional 47,000 square feet onto the asset. 

CO previously reported that, to make room for the addition, Rivani plans to cut the amount of parking spots down from 712 to 387. One hundred of those 712 spots are currently available to the public.

Rivani did not respond to requests for comment. 

Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobsrver.com.

item.title: Vaja Group to Acquire Astoria Development Site at 24-41 31st Street for $26M
item.dc:creator: Edavis
item.description: Moses Freund’s Vaja Group is set to purchase another development site along the 31st Street corridor in Astoria, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned. The developer will acquire Friday the one-story retail building at 24-41 31st Street — a former Staples location — for $26.39 million, according to broker IPRG. The 29,638-square-foot site offers nearly 150,000 buildable […]
item.content:encoded:
Moses Freund’s Vaja Group is set to purchase another development site along the 31st Street corridor in Astoria, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned. 

The developer will acquire Friday the one-story retail building at 24-41 31st Street — a former Staples location — for $26.39 million, according to broker IPRG. The 29,638-square-foot site offers nearly 150,000 buildable square feet that would support a 108-unit mixed-use development, according to IPRG’s Donal Flaherty, who represented Vaja Group. The site can also accommodate 14,000 square feet of potential retail space and parking.

Located at the corner of 31st Street and 24th Road, Vaja’s acquisition sits across 24th Road from another development site purchase — the now-demolished Neptune Diner. Vaja picked up the diner in 2025 for $11 million, according to city records, and Flaherty arranged the sale. 

Both site acquisitions were made possible by New York City’s 31st Street–Hoyt Avenue rezoning effort in 2022, which enabled a new mixed-use corridor along 31st Street.

“Scale is the hardest thing to find in Astoria,” Flaherty said in a statement. “You can buy a lot, but you can’t buy a full block with 443 feet of frontage and entitlements already in hand. Vaja understood that immediately and moved decisively.”

Earlier this year, Vaja Group also secured $84 million in bridge financing for another Astoria multifamily project, this one a 152-unit development at 11-14 35th Avenue, CO reported. 

Modern Spaces’ Evan Daniel represented the seller, 2441 Astoria Associates. The entity is part of a project team that applied to rezone and redevelop the larger 31st Street site in 2021, according to New York YIMBY, alongside MDM Development Group and 31 Neptune. 

Daniel declined to comment on the transaction, and the offices of Charles Scaturro & Sons could not be immediately reached for comment.

Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Beer-Importing Holterbosch Family Offloads LIC Warehouse for $95M
item.dc:creator: Mark Hallum
item.description: The Holterbosch family, former owners of a German beer importing and distribution business, has sold a Long Island City, Queens, warehouse a decade after the death of its patriarch. Dallas-based Ground Lease REIT, an affiliate of commercial real estate private equity firm Montgomery Street Partners, bought the property at 10-01 45th Road on the Long […]
item.content:encoded:
The Holterbosch family, former owners of a German beer importing and distribution business, has sold a Long Island City, Queens, warehouse a decade after the death of its patriarch.

Dallas-based Ground Lease REIT, an affiliate of commercial real estate private equity firm Montgomery Street Partners, bought the property at 10-01 45th Road on the Long Island City waterfront for $95 million, according to a deed filing in property records made public Thursday.

Jacob Schwimmer and JCS Realty Group entered into a lease agreement earlier in September with Montgomery and filed plans to build 495 units of housing across five buildings on the site, likely sidestepping prevailing wage requirements baked into the 485-x tax incentive, The Real Deal first reported.

It wouldn’t be the first venture together for the firms, which teamed up to buy, lease and build a mixed-use development at 138 Bruckner Boulevard in the Bronx in 2024.

The Holterbosch clan has held the Long Island City property since about 1968, public records indicate, despite the death of H. Dieter Holterbosch in 2016 at age 95. The company is named Hans Holterbosch Inc. and honors its founder who died in 1960. It is not clear if the company, once a major importer and distributor of Lowenbrau beer, is still active.

Dieter’s daughter Heidi, who seems to have been his only survivor, signed the paperwork for the deed transfer to Ground Lease REIT.

It’s unclear who brokered the deal. The Holterbosch family, which lists an office address at 375 Park Avenue, could not be reached for comment, while Ground Lease REIT did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The property along Vernon Boulevard is just feet from the Eleventh Street Basin inlet of the East River, which probably served as a logistical benefit in the past, and could also offer Ground Lease REIT development opportunities as the neighborhood continues to transform.

In 2017, Heidi Holterbosch was looking for a buyer for an 8-acre site hugging Newtown Creek at 55-01 Second Street, which had been rezoned as residential as the city prepared for the redevelopment of Hunters Point South.

Listed for $350 million, that site was eventually razed by TF Cornerstone to make way for housing developments in 2021.

Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Juanita’s Foods to Consolidate L.A. Production at 120K-SF Facility
item.dc:creator: Gregory Cornfield
item.description: An 80-year-old food manufacturer is consolidating its Southern California operations into a new 120,000-square-foot facility in Santa Fe Springs, in the first deal backed by a recently formed alliance of four Los Angeles County industrial cities. Juanita’s Foods will move production from its longtime Wilmington plant to 13100 Arctic Circle in Santa Fe Springs. The […]
item.content:encoded:
An 80-year-old food manufacturer is consolidating its Southern California operations into a new 120,000-square-foot facility in Santa Fe Springs, in the first deal backed by a recently formed alliance of four Los Angeles County industrial cities.

Juanita’s Foods will move production from its longtime Wilmington plant to 13100 Arctic Circle in Santa Fe Springs. The deal includes an incentives agreement as well as expedited permitting via the four-city partnership. Records show LBA Logistics acquired the facility in December 2019.

The cities of Commerce, Santa Fe Springs, Vernon and the City of Industry formed the Big 4 partnership in October 2025 as an economic-development coalition to coordinate investment attraction rather than compete for the same industrial employers. Together, the four cities offer about 250 million square feet of industrial space, and host more than 5,000 businesses with a workforce of about 200,000. 

The Big 4 cities estimate their combined industrial base generates roughly $33 billion in economic activity.

“This is what becomes possible when cities stop looking at economic development as a competition and start looking at it as a regional opportunity,” Santa Fe Springs City Manager René Bobadilla said in a statement. 

Juanita’s said it considered locations around the country before deciding to remain in Southern California.

“We conducted an exhaustive nationwide search before deciding where Juanita’s Foods would build its next chapter,” Chief Operating Officer Jody Jordan said. He cited Santa Fe Springs’ approach to business and the incentive package as key factors in the decision.

LBA Logistics did not immediately return a request for comment.

In May 2025, Juanita’s Foods sold a majority stake to Miami-based private equity firm Apex Capital as part of the founding De La Torre family’s estate planning. The family retained a minority interest and remains involved in operations.

Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Knighthead Lends $63M for Doral, Fla., Industrial Portfolio Buy
item.dc:creator: Andrew Coen
item.description: Midtown Capital Partners has sealed $62.92 million of acquisition financing to fund its purchase of 13 urban-infill, small-bay industrial assets in Doral, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Knighthead Funding provided the loan for Midtown’s $86 million off-market acquisition of the 290,000-square-foot portfolio spanning 13.33 acres, according to the lender. Midtown purchased the properties from Wes […]
item.content:encoded:
Midtown Capital Partners has sealed $62.92 million of acquisition financing to fund its purchase of 13 urban-infill, small-bay industrial assets in Doral, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned.

Knighthead Funding provided the loan for Midtown’s $86 million off-market acquisition of the 290,000-square-foot portfolio spanning 13.33 acres, according to the lender. Midtown purchased the properties from Wes Realty in August at a near-record industrial sales price for Miami-Dade County, The Real Deal previously reported.

The 13 properties were developed and assembled over the last 30 years, according to Knighthead, which originated the deal with a team led by Jonathan Daniel, Alexandra Wiggins and Joseph Marraccini. 

“This transaction epitomizes what we look for when financing a deal — an attractive collection of assets with significant upside in an excellent infill location,” Wiggins, vice president at Knighthead Funding, said in a statement. 

The properties, which are located west of Miami within a mile of Miami International Airport, benefit from strong demand for small-bay industrial properties in South Florida, where vacancy rates are below 3 percent, according to Knighthead. 

Arrow Real Estate Advisors arranged the debt with a team consisting of Morris Betesh, Morris Dabbah and Zach Strauss. 

“Urban-infill portfolios like this come around once in a lifetime,” Betesh, founder and managing partner at Arrow, said in a statement. “We’ve seen the small-bay industrial sector mature significantly over the last several years, and this acquisition, along with the capital markets’ reception to the transaction, is another indication of how increasingly institutional the asset class has become.” 

Midtown Capital Partners did not immediately return a request for comment.

Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Ares Management, PSP Investments Form $2.4B U.S. Logistics Partnership
item.dc:creator: Brian Pascus
item.description: Ares Management is diving deeper into the waters of U.S. logistics. The $670 billion private equity powerhouse announced Wednesday that it has formed a joint venture with Canada’s Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) to invest up to $2.4 billion into the development and acquisition of U.S. logistics facilities. Ares plans to combine its […]
item.content:encoded:
Ares Management is diving deeper into the waters of U.S. logistics. 

The $670 billion private equity powerhouse announced Wednesday that it has formed a joint venture with Canada’s Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) to invest up to $2.4 billion into the development and acquisition of U.S. logistics facilities. 

Ares plans to combine its vertically integrated logistics real estate platform, Marq Logistics, with PSP’s scaled capital to invest into “high-conviction markets” and “strategically placed logistics facilities,” according to a release. 

Dave Fazekas, head of North America logistics at Ares Real Estate, noted in a statement that his firm was motivated to invest into domestic logistics hubs due to resurgent onshoring trends, growth of digital infrastructure construction, and the economy’s ongoing reliance on e-commerce.

“We are proud to expand Ares’ long-standing relationship with PSP Investments as we leverage our collective scale and experience to identify compelling deployment opportunities and deliver value for tenants, communities and investors,” he said.

The joint venture already plans to invest in a 5.2 million-square-foot seed portfolio of 14 assets in California, Texas and New Jersey. 

Laurence Bastien, managing director of real estate investments for the Americas at PSP Investments, emphasized in a statement that the U.S. logistics sector is currently defined by “durable demand drivers and structurally constrained supply,” and the partnership with Ares provides his firm with an operating platform that will “drive value at the asset level.”

“Best-in-class operators, in sectors where our conviction is strongest — that is what our real estate strategy is built around, and this joint venture has both,” added Bastien. 

Eastdil Secured Savills acted as financial advisor on the deal.

Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Wells Fargo Refis Long Island City Apartments With $115M Fannie Mae Loan
item.dc:creator: Andrew Coen
item.description: An affiliate of Rockrose Development has secured $115 million of agency-backed debt to refinance a newly completed multifamily complex in Long Island City, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned. Wells Fargo Multifamily Capital closed the Fannie Mae-backed loan for Rockrose’s 301-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2, which opened last year in Long Island City’s Court Square […]
item.content:encoded:
An affiliate of Rockrose Development has secured $115 million of agency-backed debt to refinance a newly completed multifamily complex in Long Island City, Queens, Commercial Observer has learned.

Wells Fargo Multifamily Capital closed the Fannie Mae-backed loan for Rockrose’s 301-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2, which opened last year in Long Island City’s Court Square neighborhood. The 19-story building on 43-14 Queens Street shares a lobby and amenities with Rockrose’s adjacent 790-unit Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 1 tower. 

Avison Young negotiated the debt with a tri-state debt and equity finance team consisting of  Scott Singer, Andy Singer, Kevin Swartz and Kathleen McSharry.

“Long Island City remains one of the region’s most compelling multifamily markets, driven by strong residential demand, extraordinarily convenient transportation, and ongoing neighborhood growth,” Scott Singer, principal at Avison Young, said in a statement. “Phase 2 has further elevated Rockrose’s earlier Phase 1 of the Eagle Lofts Collection.”

Seventy percent of apartments at Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2 are market rate with 30 percent of the units designated as affordable housing. The property’s amenities include a spa with saunas, a bowling alley, a golf simulator and a rooftop pool.

Wells Fargo originated the loan with a team led by Pete Cannava, head of multifamily capital and community lending and Investment; Philip Maniscalco, head of production for multifamily capital; and Brian Antonuccio, head of East Coast production.

“With 301 new residences, nearly a third of them affordable, Eagle Lofts Collection, Phase 2 meaningfully expands housing access in Long Island City,” Maniscalco said in a statement. 

Richard Brancato, chief operating officer at Rockrose, said in a statement, the transaction “reflects the strength” of its “long-standing relationships” with Wells Fargo and Avison Young. 

Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Borough Developers Closes on $84M Sale of Downtown Brooklyn Development Site
item.dc:creator: Isabelle Durso
item.description: Brooklyn-based Borough Developers has acquired a major mixed-use development site in Downtown Brooklyn, right across from the new retail project at a former Macy’s, Commercial Observer has learned. The firm acquired 485 Fulton Street and 147 Lawrence Street — a 33,153-square-foot site known as the Bridge & Fulton Development Site — from ICER Real Estate […]
item.content:encoded:
Brooklyn-based Borough Developers has acquired a major mixed-use development site in Downtown Brooklyn, right across from the new retail project at a former Macy’s, Commercial Observer has learned.

The firm acquired 485 Fulton Street and 147 Lawrence Street — a 33,153-square-foot site known as the Bridge & Fulton Development Site — from ICER Real Estate for $83.5 million, according to JLL, which brokered the deal for both sides.

Borough Developers secured an $85 million acquisition and pre-development loan from BridgeCity Capital for the deal.

“The transaction closed in just 16 days, underscoring our ability to move quickly and execute under tight deadlines,” EJ Ehrlich, director of originations at BridgeCity, said in a statement to CO. “This transaction reflects our continued ability to structure and execute complex financing solutions for high-quality development sites across New York City.”

Last month, Shimon Kleinman, co-founder of Borough Developers, filed plans with the New York City Department of Buildings to build a trio of 99-unit residential buildings on the site, meaning the developer is likely trying to utilize the state’s 485-x tax abatement program. That program comes with steeper construction wage requirements for projects of 100 units or more.

Kleinman’s initial filing would see a total of 297 housing units built on the site, but BridgeCity said the building is set to comprise a total of 468 residential units, commercial space and amenities. JLL, which said the planned number of units is subject to change, said the project will include four buildings comprising retail on the ground floor and residential units above.

The development site has 350,000 buildable square feet. The existing 139,438-square-foot building on the property — currently home to a barber shop — will be demolished to make way for the new housing, according to JLL.

JLL’s Ethan Stanton, Michael Mazzara and Brendan Maddigan represented the seller and the buyer.

“This sale speaks to the continued strength of investor conviction in Downtown Brooklyn and, more broadly, the value developers are placing on well-located sites where they can build housing at meaningful scale,” Mazzara said in a statement. “There are very few opportunities of this size in a neighborhood with this level of transit access, residential demand and established retail. The combination of scale, location and development flexibility made 485 Fulton particularly compelling.”

Kao Hwa Lee Architects is the registered architect on Kleinman’s filed plans for the project. A spokesperson for the architecture firm did not immediately respond to a request for comment, while Borough Developers could not be reached for comment.

The planned mixed-use development is directly across the street from the former Macy’s department store at 422 Fulton Street, which is being renovated into a five-floor retail and entertainment spot called BKX.

Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: Capital Insight Acquires Hudson Yards Hotel Property in Foreclosure Auction
item.dc:creator: Mark Hallum
item.description: Capital Insight has acquired a former hotel with retail and parking in Manhattan’s Hudson Yards for somewhere between $68 million and $71.3 million, according to court records. Investment banking business Capital Insight — the former lender and debt holder on the property — took ownership of the 12-story building at 511 Ninth Avenue through a […]
item.content:encoded:
Capital Insight has acquired a former hotel with retail and parking in Manhattan’s Hudson Yards for somewhere between $68 million and $71.3 million, according to court records. 

Investment banking business Capital Insight — the former lender and debt holder on the property — took ownership of the 12-story building at 511 Ninth Avenue through a foreclosure auction. The auction occurred after Assa Properties fell into financial troubles associated with the property and the site went to special servicing through CW Capital Asset Management.

Capital Insight and CW Capital did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

PincusCo first reported the foreclosure auction, saying Capital Insight was expected to use the property as a cash-flowing asset with its six commercial condominiums.

Assa planned the Ninth Avenue development as a combination hotel-multifamily property branded as Galerie515 Hotel & Condominium Residences when construction first began in 2012. The residential portion was also named Lana at some point, and the Cassa Hotel Times Square portion closed in 2020.

A new steakhouse named Vida Steakhouse is set to open in the retail space at 511 Ninth Avenue next year, but it’s unclear if that lease will proceed under new ownership.

Assa Properties, owned by the Assa family and led by founder Solly Assa, could not be reached for comment.

The most recent property records linking the ownership to the Assa family date back to 2014, with filings linked to Cassa Capital, one of Assa’s other organizations, through an address at 410 Park Avenue.

Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

item.title: ACORE Claims Keys to Would-be Life Sciences Facility in Hell’s Kitchen
item.dc:creator: Edavis
item.description: The lender behind Georgetown Company and Beacon Capital Partners’ planned life sciences facility at 707 11th Avenue and 615 West 50th Street in Hell’s Kitchen has reclaimed the keys. ACORE Capital received the unconverted office properties through a deed in lieu of foreclosure valued at $60 million, according to city records filed Wednesday. ACORE’s Jason […]
item.content:encoded:
The lender behind Georgetown Company and Beacon Capital Partners’ planned life sciences facility at 707 11th Avenue and 615 West 50th Street in Hell’s Kitchen has reclaimed the keys.

Acore Capital received the unconverted office properties through a deed in lieu of foreclosure valued at $60 million, according to city records filed Wednesday. ACORE’s Jason Mann, a managing director, signed on behalf of the new ownership entity, Wexford Investment Trust.

John Lawrence, senior managing director at Beacon, signed Wednesday’s property transfer on behalf of the developer. Georgetown sold its interest in the properties to Beacon earlier this year and has not been involved in the project since, a spokesperson for Georgetown told Commercial Observer.

Georgetown and Beacon acquired the next-door buildings near the corner of 11th Avenue and West 50th Street in 2021, Commercial Observer reported, paying SL Green Realty $95 million. The larger building at 707 11th Avenue previously housed the headquarters of clothing and accessories retailer Kenneth Cole.

Plans were filed in early 2023 to replace the office properties with a seven-story life sciences facility. The development would have featured laboratory, research and office spaces, according to New York YIMBY, and would have been Manhattan’s first ground-up, purpose-built life science property in a decade.  

Georgetown and Beacon’s ambitious plans did not progress beyond pre-development, and ACORE filed a pre-foreclosure action against ownership in April, PincusCo reported. ACORE Capital, acting as the lender’s administrative agent, claimed the owners had fallen behind on a $60 million debt.

Multiple Manhattan facilities planned in the years immediately following the 2020 pandemic have changed hands in recent weeks and months. On the Upper East Side, Taconic Partners’ stalled Iron Horse Labs project at 309 East 94th Street sold to multifamily developer LCOR for $73 million, CO reported on Friday. Taconic’s West End Labs at 125 West End Avenue also sold in July to Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square Foundation for $188 million. 

Post-pandemic vacancies still weigh on the U.S. life sciences sector. In New York City, leasing volume dived 84 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the previous year, according to CBRE data.

Spokespeople for Beacon and ACORE did not respond to requests for comment. 

Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.

Update: This article has been updated to reflect the earlier sale of Georgetown’s interest in the properties.
